85.title: Paul in Athens (Acts 17:16–34)
85.hook: he quotes their own poets: in him we live and move and have our being
85.howItsDone: Christians often point to Paul's speech on the Areopagus as a model for speaking respectfully with people of other views. The line 'in him we live, and move, and have our being' is widely used in prayers and hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lydia and the jailer, and two men singing in the stocks. Your line was sing at midnight. What did you hum in a dark moment? Day eighty-five.

Think of the last time you talked with someone who sees the world very differently from you. At a wedding, maybe, or in a comment thread. Where did you start? Most of us start with where they're wrong. Now go to Athens, the most famous city of ideas in the ancient world. Paul is there alone, waiting for his friends. He walks the streets, and he's deeply stirred: the city is full of statues and altars to many gods, and he's a Jew who worships one. He talks in the synagogue, and in the marketplace with anyone who'll listen, including philosophers from two big schools, the Stoics and the Epicureans. Some call him a babbler. Others are curious. So they bring him up to the Areopagus, the hill where the city's council met, and say: tell us this new thing.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU START?` → `A CITY OF IDEAS.` → `UP TO THE AREOPAGUS.`

segments.voice: Paul begins, surprisingly, with a compliment. I see you're a very religious people, he says. Walking around, I found an altar with this inscription, in the King James Bible: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD." He doesn't mock it. He starts from it. The one you honor without knowing, he says, that's the one I'm telling you about: the God who made the world, who doesn't live in buildings made by hands, and who isn't far from any of us. And then he does something no one expects from a traveling Jewish teacher. He quotes their own poets: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." The second line comes from Aratus, a Greek poet who lived about three centuries earlier. The first is often credited to another old Greek poet, Epimenides, though scholars aren't sure. Either way, Paul stands on their hill and speaks their language, quoting the books on their shelves. Then he gets to his own center: a day of judgment, and a man raised from the dead. That's where the room splits. When they hear about resurrection, some laugh at him. Others say, politely, we'll hear you again about this. And a few believe, and Luke names two: Dionysius, a member of the council, and a woman named Damaris. Christians have pointed to this speech for centuries as a way to talk across a gap: start with what's good and true in the other person's world, honor it, and then say plainly what you believe. And the line from the poets became one of the most loved in the whole New Testament. In him we live.
screen: `TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` · `HE STARTS FROM WHAT THEY HAVE.` · `QUOTING THEIR OWN POETS.` · `SOME LAUGH. SOME STAY.` · then, large: `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one good thing in a stranger's view. Sit, and breathe. Think of a view you don't share. A politics, a faith, a way of raising kids, a way of spending money. Picture someone who holds it. Now look for their altar to the unknown god: the thing they're reaching for that you can honor. Safety, maybe. Fairness. Freedom. Love for their family. Name it to yourself, kindly. You don't have to agree with them. Just find the good. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Paul in Athens. An altar to an unknown god, two lines from Greek poets, and a speech that began with a compliment.
Your line: in him we live. Today, in one disagreement, name something true on the other side before you say anything else. Tomorrow, two weeks of storm at sea. Day eighty-five.

86.title: The shipwreck (Acts 27–28)
86.hook: two weeks of storm, Paul breaks bread on deck, 276 swim to Malta, and a viper bites harmlessly
86.howItsDone: Many Christians give thanks before meals, as Paul does on the deck. In Malta, Paul's shipwreck is remembered every February 10 with a public holiday and feast, and many Maltese Christians trace their faith to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul in Athens, quoting the poets on their own hill. Your line was in him we live. What good did you find on the other side? Day eighty-six.

Some weeks are all storm. One thing breaks, then another, and you stop being able to see the sky. Now picture a cargo ship in the Mediterranean, late in the sailing season. On board is Paul, not as a passenger but as a prisoner, being taken to Rome for trial under a Roman officer named Julius. Paul warns them it's too late in the year to sail on. Nobody listens. Then a violent wind comes down off the island of Crete, the ship is caught, and they can't turn her into it. They lash ropes around the hull to hold it together. They throw the cargo overboard, then the ship's gear. For day after day there's no sun, no stars. And Luke, who writes this part as we, as if he's on board, says all hope that we should be saved was taken away.
screen: `A PRISONER ON A CARGO SHIP.` → `THE WIND OFF CRETE.` → `NO SUN, NO STARS.`

segments.voice: In the middle of it, Paul stands up among the exhausted crew and says, in the King James Bible: "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship." An angel stood by me last night, he says. And again: "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God." Be of good cheer is the old English for today's line. The Greek means something like be good-spirited. Take heart. On the fourteenth night they sense land is near. Some sailors try to slip away in the lifeboat, and are stopped. And just before dawn, with everyone starving and terrified, Paul does the most ordinary thing. He tells them to eat. You've gone two weeks without a real meal, he says, and this is for your health. Then, Luke says, "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." Took, gave thanks, broke. The same words as the Last Supper and the road to Emmaus, now on the deck of a sinking ship, among soldiers, sailors and prisoners. And they all take heart and eat. Luke even gives the head count: two hundred and seventy-six people. At daybreak the ship runs aground and breaks apart. Those who can swim jump first; the rest float in on planks. Every one of them reaches the shore. It's Malta, and the islanders build a fire in the cold rain. A viper comes out of the firewood and fastens onto Paul's hand. The locals decide he must be a murderer. He shakes it into the fire, and nothing happens. So they change their minds and decide he's a god.
screen: `BE OF GOOD CHEER.` · `THIS IS FOR YOUR HEALTH.` · `HE TOOK BREAD, AND GAVE THANKS.` · `276, ALL SAFE TO LAND.` · then, large: `TAKE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something steadying in a hard week. If you have something near you, a piece of bread, a cracker, fruit, a cup of tea, take it now. If not, just picture it. Before you eat, stop. Hold it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it, as Paul did on the deck. If you don't, just notice where it came from, and how many hands it passed through. Then eat it slowly, the way someone eats who hasn't eaten properly in a while. Let your body be steadied, one bite at a time. The bell holds the time.
The shipwreck. Fourteen days of storm, bread broken on a sinking deck, and two hundred and seventy-six people safe on Malta.
Your line: take heart. Today, in the storm of the week, eat one proper meal, sitting down, and let it steady you. Tomorrow, Paul's letters as real mail. Day eighty-six.

87.title: The letters as letters
87.hook: Paul's letters are real post: greetings, travel plans, and a list of friends' names (Romans 16)
87.howItsDone: In most churches a reading from one of the New Testament letters, often called the Epistle, is read aloud at Sunday worship, the way the letters were first heard by the churches they were sent to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shipwreck: bread broken on a sinking deck, and everyone safe on Malta. Your line was take heart. What steadied you this week? Day eighty-seven.

Think of the last real letter you got. Not an email. Paper. Maybe a card from a grandparent, with the news, a little advice, and a list at the end: say hi to your mom, love to the kids. Now think about the Bible. A lot of the New Testament, thirteen of its twenty-seven books, carry Paul's name, and they're not essays or sermons. They're letters. Real mail, sent to real people in real cities: Rome, Corinth, Philippi, Thessalonica. Somebody carried them by hand, over roads and seas, and somebody read them aloud to a room full of people who knew the sender. And if you read to the very end of the longest one, Romans, you find something most people skip right over.
screen: `A REAL LETTER, ON PAPER.` → `THIRTEEN LETTERS, ONE NAME.` → `READ TO THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: Today's word is epistle, from the Greek for something sent. And Paul's letters follow the shape of any letter of his day: who it's from, who it's to, a greeting, grace and peace, then thanks, then the business, then travel plans, then hellos. Romans chapter sixteen is almost all hellos. It opens, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Phoebe was very likely the one carrying the letter. Then comes a list of more than twenty-five names. "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," a married couple who risked their necks for him, with a church meeting in their house. Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with him. Tryphena and Tryphosa, who work hard. Rufus, and his mother, who was a mother to Paul too. Some are Jewish names, some Greek, some Latin, some common slave names. Women and men, side by side. And then, near the end, a different voice breaks in: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Tertius is the scribe, writing it all down as Paul speaks, and he adds his own hello. In other letters Paul takes the pen at the end and signs in his own big handwriting. In one he asks a friend to bring the coat he left behind, and his books. Why does this matter? Because the letters people now read in church as scripture started out as mail between friends. Christians hear them as God speaking. And they never stopped being letters, full of names.
screen: `EPISTLE: SOMETHING SENT.` · `PHOEBE CARRIES THE LETTER.` · `TWENTY-FIVE NAMES AND MORE.` · `I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS.` · then, large: `NAMES MATTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one real letter or card. For now, just begin it in your head. Sit, and breathe. Choose one person who'd be surprised to hear from you. Start the way Paul did: who it's from, who it's to, a greeting. Then say one specific thing you're grateful for about them. Then some ordinary news. Then a list: who else should they say hello to for you? Use names. If you pray, you can pray for each name as it comes. Later today, write it down, and send it. The bell holds the time.
Epistle. From the Greek for something sent. Paul's letters: real mail, full of travel plans, a scribe's hello, and friends' names.
Your line: names matter. Today, send the letter or card, and put at least one name in it besides theirs. Tomorrow, Paul's shortest letter, about a runaway. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: Philemon
88.hook: a short note asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother
88.carry: no longer a servant, but a brother
88.howItsDone: Philemon is read in churches as a letter about reconciliation and about how faith changes relationships of power. It was also central in debates over slavery, when abolitionists and defenders of slavery read it in opposite ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the epistle: Paul's letters as real mail, with a scribe's hello and a list of friends. Your line was names matter. Whose name went into your card? Day eighty-eight.

Have you ever had to write a note on someone else's behalf? A reference. A text to smooth things over between two friends. You choose every word, because someone's future is riding on it. Paul's shortest letter is exactly that. It fits on a single page. It's written from prison to a man named Philemon, a believer with a church meeting in his home. And it's about a young man named Onesimus. Onesimus is enslaved in Philemon's household, and he has left it. Somewhere along the way he found Paul, in prison, and became a believer. Now Paul is sending him back, carrying this letter. Philemon has the law on his side, and the power to punish. Everything depends on the words on this page.
screen: `A NOTE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `ONE PAGE, FROM PRISON.` → `ONESIMUS GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: Listen to how Paul does it. He says he could order Philemon to do the right thing, but he'd rather appeal, for love's sake. He calls Onesimus my son, my very heart. And he makes a joke, because the name Onesimus means useful: "Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me." Then he says what he's really asking. Take him back, the King James Bible says, "Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved." The word the old English translates as servant is doulos, which means slave. Paul is asking a slave owner to receive an enslaved man as a brother, in the flesh, as well as in the Lord. Then he signs a blank check: "If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account." I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it. And he ends, knowing you'll do even more than I say. Now the honest part. The letter never says, in so many words, set him free, and it doesn't tell us why Onesimus left, or what Philemon did next. The Bible is silent. Over the centuries, some Christians used Paul's letters to defend slavery, and others, including many who fought to end it, read this page as pointing the other way: once a man is your brother, how can he be your property? A few decades later, a bishop of Ephesus was named Onesimus. Some have wondered if it was the same man. Nobody knows. What we have is one page, where Paul puts his own name on the line for someone with less power, and asks for a new word: brother.
screen: `FOR LOVE'S SAKE, NOT ORDERS.` · `ONESIMUS MEANS USEFUL.` · `PUT THAT ON MINE ACCOUNT.` · `THE BIBLE IS SILENT ON WHAT CAME NEXT.` · then, large: `A BROTHER BELOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak up for someone with less power. Sit, and breathe. Think of someone in your world who has less say than the people around them. A new employee. A kid. Someone who cleans the office after everyone leaves. Someone whose English is still new. Is there a word you could put in for them, the way Paul did? A thank you said where the boss can hear. A good reference. Putting something on your account. Picture doing it. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Philemon. Paul's shortest letter, asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother.
Your line: no longer a servant, but a brother. Today, put in one good word for someone with less power, where it counts. Tomorrow, a letter to a quarrelling church. Day eighty-eight.

89.title: Love is patient (1 Corinthians 13)
89.hook: written to a quarrelling church, not a wedding: love is patient, kind, not puffed up
89.howItsDone: 1 Corinthians 13 is one of the most frequently read passages at Christian weddings and funerals, and churches also read it in Sunday worship. Many Christians memorize its description of love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philemon, and a page asking for a new word. Your line was no longer a servant, but a brother. Who did you put in a good word for? Day eighty-nine.
screen: `NO LONGER A SERVANT, BUT A BROTHER.`

segments.voice: You've heard it at a wedding. Someone's cousin walks up to the microphone, a little nervous, and reads: love is patient, love is kind. Everyone smiles at the couple. It's beautiful there. But that's not where it was first read. It was first read out loud to a church in Corinth, a busy port city in Greece, and that church was a mess. They'd split into fan clubs: I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, I follow Peter. Members were taking each other to court. At their shared meals, the wealthy ate first and the poor went home hungry. And they were competing over whose spiritual gifts were the most impressive. Paul writes them a long letter, and right in the middle of the argument, he stops, and writes this.
screen: `READ AT A WEDDING.` → `WRITTEN TO A MESS.` → `FAN CLUBS AND LAWSUITS.`

segments.voice: It starts with a warning to the show-offs, in the King James Bible: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." Impressive, and just noise. Then comes the part we know: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." The King James says charity, from the Latin caritas. The Greek word underneath is today's word: agape. It isn't the word for romance, or for friendship. It's the love that wills the good of the other, even when they're difficult. Christians say it's the love God has for the world. Now read it again, knowing who it was for. Suffers long: to a church where people kept suing each other. Envies not: to people jealous of each other's gifts. Not puffed up: earlier in the same letter Paul has already told them, knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Every line is a mirror held up to a quarreling room. It's not a greeting card. It's a correction, written with great tenderness. Paul goes on: love never fails; everything else we have is partial, for now we see through a glass, darkly. And he ends: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Churches still read it at weddings, and it belongs there too. But it was written for the hardest kind of love: loving people you're in the middle of a fight with. Which is also, as it happens, what a marriage needs.
screen: `SOUNDING BRASS, TINKLING CYMBAL.` · `AGAPE: LOVE THAT WILLS YOUR GOOD.` · `A MIRROR TO A QUARRELING ROOM.` · `FAITH, HOPE, CHARITY.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST OF THESE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with one difficult person. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who tries your patience. Picture them clearly: their voice, their habits, the thing they always do. Now take one line of Paul's and hold it up against yourself, not them. Suffers long. Is kind. Is not puffed up. Which one is hardest with this person? Just notice. Then imagine the next time you see them, and one small way to be patient. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Agape. The Greek word for love that wills the good of the other; charity in the King James. The last word of our stretch through Acts and Paul's letters.
Your line: the greatest of these. Today, when the difficult person does the thing, let love suffer long, for one more minute. Tomorrow, the saints begin. Day eighty-nine.

90.title: What a saint is
90.hook: Paul calls every believer a saint; Catholics and Orthodox also honor holy people named by the church
90.howItsDone: Christians confess 'the communion of saints' in the Apostles' Creed. Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask the saints to pray for them and keep their feast days; Anglicans and Lutherans keep saints' calendars; many Protestants call every believer a saint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, agape, love that suffers long, written to a quarreling church. Your line was the greatest of these. How did one more minute of patience go? Day ninety.

When you hear the word saint, what comes to mind? Maybe a stained-glass window, someone with a golden circle around their head. Maybe a city: San Francisco, Saint Louis, São Paulo. Maybe an eye-roll: well, I'm no saint. We use it for people impossibly better than us. Now remember yesterday's church in Corinth: the fan clubs, the lawsuits, the rich eating first while the poor went hungry. How does Paul address his letter to them? To the church of God at Corinth, to them that are, as the King James puts it, called to be saints. That church. Those people. This week, the last of our stories, we'll meet some saints as real characters. But first, what the word actually means.
screen: `A GOLDEN CIRCLE, A CITY, AN EYE-ROLL.` → `I'M NO SAINT.` → `THE CORINTHIANS: CALLED TO BE SAINTS.`

segments.voice: The Greek word is hagios, and it means holy, set apart, belonging to God. The Latin is sanctus, and that gives us saint. In the New Testament it isn't a prize for the best people; it's a name for all of them. Paul opens his letter to Rome, in the King James Bible: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints." To Philippi: to all the saints in Christ Jesus. Every believer, in every messy church. Holy not because they'd earned it, but because God had claimed them. Ordinary people, made holy. Then, over the centuries, Christians also began to honor particular people whose lives shone: martyrs first, then teachers, monks, mothers, reformers of the poor. And here the churches take different paths. Catholics recognize saints through a formal process called canonization, and ask the saints in heaven to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. Orthodox Christians honor saints in icons and hymns, and also ask their prayers. Anglicans and Lutherans keep calendars of saints' days and remember them as examples. And many other Protestants use the word mostly Paul's way, for every believer, and honor heroes of the faith without asking for their prayers. What all of them share is a line from the old creed: the communion of saints, the belief that God's people, living and dead, belong together. The letter to the Hebrews pictures it as a stadium: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." And many churches keep All Saints' Day, November first, for the famous and the forgotten alike.
screen: `HAGIOS: SET APART FOR GOD.` · `PAUL: EVERY BELIEVER.` · `HOLY PEOPLE, HONORED DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.` · then, large: `ORDINARY PEOPLE, MADE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one person whose goodness helped you. Sit, and breathe. Let your mind go back through your life, and find one person. Not famous. Maybe not even religious. A teacher who noticed you. A neighbor who fed you. A grandparent. Someone whose plain goodness reached you. Picture their face. Say their name, quietly, out loud. Let yourself be grateful. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If they're still alive, you might tell them one day. The bell holds the time.
Saint. From the Latin sanctus, holy. In Paul's letters, every believer; in the churches' calendars, holy lives remembered.
Your line: ordinary people, made holy. Today, notice one ordinary person doing one good thing, and let yourself see it as holy. Tomorrow, a mother who wouldn't stop crying for her son. Day ninety.

original.note: Greek: holy, set apart, belonging to God. Paul's word for every believer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint is someone far better than you.
what it means: in Paul's letters, every believer is a saint, holy because God has claimed them; later, churches also honored particular holy lives.

91.title: Monica's tears
91.hook: a mother prays for years for her wayward son, Augustine, and a bishop tells her such tears won't be lost
91.howItsDone: Saint Monica is honored as a patron of mothers and of those who pray for loved ones who have drifted from faith. In the Catholic calendar her feast is August 27, the day before Saint Augustine's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saint: every believer, in Paul's letters, and holy lives remembered. Your line was ordinary people, made holy. Whose ordinary goodness did you notice? Thirteen weeks on the path. Day ninety-one.

If you've ever loved someone who kept making the choice you were afraid of, you know this feeling. You lie awake. You rehearse the conversation. You try again, and it goes badly again. North Africa, about sixteen hundred years ago. A woman named Monica has a son who is brilliant, charming, ambitious, and restless. His name is Augustine. He drifts from the faith she raised him in, throws himself into success, and into a way of life that breaks her heart. She weeps for him, prays for him, and follows him around. Years go by. We know all this because, decades later, Augustine told the story himself, in a book addressed to God, called the Confessions. And he doesn't spare himself.
screen: `AWAKE AT NIGHT.` → `A BRILLIANT, RESTLESS SON.` → `HE TOLD IT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: At one point, Monica goes to a bishop and begs him to talk sense into her son. The bishop says no. He's not ready, the bishop says; leave him alone and keep praying; he'll find his own way. She won't take no. She keeps pleading, in floods of tears. And finally the bishop, a bit worn out, says to her, go your way, it cannot be that the son of these tears should perish. Augustine says his mother took that as if it had sounded from heaven. It didn't fix anything quickly. When Augustine decided to sail for Rome, he lied to her to slip away, and left her weeping on the shore. So she followed him, across the sea, all the way to Milan. And there, finally, the road turned. Augustine was baptized by the bishop of Milan, Ambrose, at Easter, in the year 387. Not long after, mother and son stood at a window in the port town of Ostia, near Rome, talking quietly about God, and Augustine describes it as the two of them touching something eternal for a moment. A few days later she fell ill and died, far from home, content. The son of those tears became one of the most influential Christian thinkers who ever lived. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and many Protestant Christians read him still. Churches honor Monica as a saint, and in the Catholic calendar her feast is August twenty-seventh, the day before his. Christians have held on to her story for the plainest reason: it says that years of tears, poured out for someone who seems not to be listening, are not wasted.
screen: `THE BISHOP SAYS NO.` · `THE SON OF THESE TEARS.` · `SHE FOLLOWS HIM TO MILAN.` · `A WINDOW AT OSTIA.` · then, large: `TEARS ARE NOT WASTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone you've nearly given up on. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've been worrying over for a long time. The one who never calls back. The one who keeps choosing the thing that hurts them. Let yourself feel it, even if tears come. If you pray, you can bring them to God in whatever words you have, or none. If you don't pray, just hold them in your mind with love, the way Monica did, for two minutes. Don't try to fix them. Just don't let go. The bell holds the time.
Monica's tears. A mother's long, stubborn love, and a bishop's promise. This week: Athens, a shipwreck, an epistle, Philemon, agape, saint, and Monica.

Your line: tears are not wasted. Today, send one small sign of love to the person you're worried about, without a lecture attached. Tomorrow, her son hears a child's voice in a garden. Day ninety-one.
